A step function is a function that can be written as a finite linear combination of indicator functions of intervals. Since a step function is bounded, it is Riemann Integrable. Additionally, since a step function has at most a countable number of discontinuities, it is also Riemann Integrable.

Here is a more formal proof:

Let f be a step function / [a, b] -> \mathbb{R}. Then, there exists a finite set of points {x_1, x_2,..., x_n} in [a, b] such that f(x) = c_i for x in [x_i, x_{i+1}) for i = 1, 2,..., n-1, and f(x) = c_n for x in [x_n, b].

Since f is bounded, there exists a real number M such that |f(x)| <= M for all x in [a, b]. This implies that f is Riemann Integrable.

To show that f has at most a countable number of discontinuities, suppose that f has a discontinuity at x. Then, there exists an \epsilon > 0 such that |f(x + \epsilon) - f(x - \epsilon)| > 2M. Since f is a step function, there exists an i such that x \in [x_i, x_{i+1}) and f(x) = c_i. Then, x + \epsilon \in [x_{i+1}, x_{i+2}) and f(x + \epsilon) = c_{i+1}. Since f is a step function, there exists a point y in [x_{i+1}, x_{i+2}) such that f(y) = c_i. Then, |f(x + \epsilon) - f(x - \epsilon)| = |c_{i+1} - c_i| <= M, which contradicts the assumption that |f(x + \epsilon) - f(x - \epsilon)| > 2M. Therefore, f has at most a countable number of discontinuities.

Since f is bounded and has at most a countable number of discontinuities, it is Riemann Integrable.

Note that this proof assumes that the step function is defined on a closed interval [a, b]. If the step function is defined on an open interval (a, b), then it is not Riemann Integrable.
